title: Swimming Upstream
full_review:
Bravura performances by Geoffrey Rush and Judy Davis, and a story of professional triumph over domestic adversity, don't entirely compensate for the sordidness of this true-life story of Australian swimming champion Tony Fingleton in "Swimming Upstream" (MGM).

Directed by Russell Mulcahy from a script by Fingleton, the film charts Tony's progress from young boy to world-class swimmer under the resolutely disapproving eye of a father who doesn't love him.

The film -- based on a book by Fingleton, co-written with his sister, Diane -- begins in the 1950s, and young Tony is living with his siblings, including the brutish Harold Jr. and kindly John, and their parents, the alcoholic wharf laborer Harold (Geoffrey Rush) and the long-suffering and loving Dora (Judy Davis). The father clearly favors the macho, bullying Harold Jr., whom he sees as epitomizing what a man should be. Harold Jr. torments Tony relentlessly, even slamming down a piano lid on Tony's hands while he's playing.

Dora is supportive of Tony, whose artistic leanings (besides playing the piano, he reads Shakespeare) are despised by the father who sees them as marks of effeminacy. (In a later scene, Harold will snatch "Hamlet" from Tony's hands and disdainfully toss it in the swimming pool.)

Dora urges Tony to be "strong in the head" to protect himself from his father's continual belittling. She also reinforces the fact that only he has the internal capacity to make something of his life, rather than relying on his father or even her.

One day Harold accompanies Tony and John to the local pool, where unbeknownst to him, they have become amazingly proficient.

Harold watches with calculating wonderment, and from that point on, shifts his sights to training John and Tony, pushing them almost beyond endurance, as he watches from the sidelines with a keen eye. John is clearly his favorite, though, and Harold repeatedly shows lack of interest in any of Tony's triumphs.

Years pass, and the two boys are good enough to enter competitions. John scores an early victory, but eventually, much to the father's disdain, it is Tony who moves out in front.

The father leans on John to persevere, and under his father's urging, secretly enters a race against his brother, but eventually Tony comes out on top again, causing a rift between the two brothers, once so close.

Harold frequently becomes seriously violent, striking anyone in his way, including Dora. The children urge her to escape the never-ending pattern of abuse, but Dora can't bring herself to break free and even attempts to take her own life.

As Tony goes from triumph to triumph, it's clear he's desperately seeking his father's love, but Harold, infuriatingly, refuses or is incapable of giving it.

The father's malice is puzzling. He calls his son a "poufter," but does he really think the boy is gay? Though we learn he had a horrific childhood -- his mother having sexual encounters with strangers who, it is implied, also abused him -- Harold's unaccountable resentment (or, at best, indifference) to Tony, particularly after the latter's success, is as puzzling as it is ultimately tiresome for the viewer.

By the end, we're supposed to feel some pity for the father, but he still emerges as pretty despicable, in spite of Rush's nuanced portrayal.

You root for Tony to get away from his intolerable home life, but his ultimate decision to go to Harvard seems more a case of running away from a miserable situation than a wholly positive achievement. Yet Tony's understanding and ultimate rapprochement with his father and bullying brother, and Dora's loving devotion to Tony and empathy for her husband deliver the right message.

Rush adds another indelible portrait to his gallery of screen performances. And it's good to have Davis back on her native Aussie ground, after her triumphs as Judy Garland and Nancy Reagan on American television. Her distinctly unfeminist devotion to her husband and compassion for his son bear the authentic ring of truth for a housewife of that era.

Jesse Spencer (who portrays Tony), Tim Draxl (John) and David Hoflin (Harold Jr.) are good as the brothers, and well-matched by Mitchell Dellevergin, Thomas Davidson and Kain O'Keefe as their younger selves.

Mulcahy directs this slice-of-life drama with a sure hand, and uses a split screen sportslike technique for the swimming scenes and fanciful water imagery, which adds visual variety.

Overall, this schizophrenic film is more of a "Daddy Dearest" downer than the "Chariots of Fire" type of tale that it might have been, but Rush and Davis are reason enough to see it.

The film contains many scenes of domestic violence, heavy drinking, a smattering of rough and crude language, a suicide attempt and some sexual references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
